toc.title: One: what you have access to
Two: what you learned growing up

blocks.p: A listener sent me a question that I want to take on. It's a complex one, and these are my thoughts as they come to me, not a fully worked-out answer. Here's what they wrote:

q: Why do some people become sex addicts, whereas some become drug addicts and some become food addicts? It's trauma for all addictions at a fundamental level, but what variable in trauma distinguishes whether an individual is susceptible to sexual addiction versus food addiction versus substance addiction?

blocks.p: It's obviously more than one factor. Here are a few of the probably many factors that play into it.

blocks.h: One: what you have access to

blocks.p: The first factor is pretty obvious: what do you have access to? It's hard to become addicted to food if you don't have food to get addicted to. It's hard to become addicted to a drug if you don't have that drug. I don't think I need to go deeper into that one.

blocks.h: Two: what you learned growing up

blocks.p: Another factor is what you learned, based on your context, about how to deal with your feelings, your stuck defensive state, your trauma. Probably growing up. What did you learn from the people in your life who were supposed to model these things? What did they show you about how you're supposed to deal with your stuff, or not deal with your stuff?

If you were raised around someone who is an alcoholic, that may teach you that the way to deal with your feelings is alcohol specifically, or maybe substance use in general, and maybe you end up with something else. It's not uncommon for children of alcoholics to grow up, use alcohol as a way to deal with their feelings, then look back and say, "Oh my God, I'm doing the same thing." That may simply be what you learned as a way to deal with your stuff. Or, I guess, not deal with your stuff.

Part of what we learn growing up isn't just what works. It's also what is not acceptable. Culturally, based on family, based on church, whatever it is, what did you learn was not okay? You may have learned that being thin was acceptable, or even applauded, while also learning that drug use, substance use, alcohol use was not acceptable and not applauded.

So when it comes to dealing with your own stuff, what you learned was okay and not okay can come into play: this thing over here is shameful, and this thing over here might get me ostracized in some way, but this other thing is something people will actually admire about me. It helps relieve what I'm going through, and people might admire it, or at least it's socially acceptable in whatever context I'm in.

The third factor is what you got exposed to that kind of worked. By worked, I mean what provided enough relief or escape. Neither word is quite right. I think relief is different when it doesn't come from a behavioral adaptation. Maybe rewarding is a better word: what was rewarding enough, in the face of your stuck defensive state, that it made you seek it out again?

I'm just making this up, but say someone has stuck freeze energy, with a lot of panic inside of them. When they smoke marijuana, it might calm them down, and they get the sense of relief they need. They get some sort of escape, relief, whatever it is, from that stuck, panicky flavor of freeze, from that trauma energy.

Now, if that same person tried meth or alcohol or whatever, it may not give them the same sense of relief. It may amp them up. It may turn them into a person they don't want to be. Maybe it amps up their anger.

Likewise, for somebody in a stuck shutdown state, smoking marijuana may not be what they're searching for. Getting addicted to caffeine, though, might be an escape from their shutdown state. Maybe it gives them motivation. Maybe it helps them feel energized, and that's more rewarding for what they want than another avenue.

I don't know the chemical makeup of all this stuff, and I can't go into that. Of course these things are physically and biologically reinforcing, absolutely. I just don't have the knowledge to talk about that in depth. I'm talking about it behaviorally, psychologically, emotionally: did you get what you wanted or not? This one avenue was more of a relief, or more rewarding, than another avenue.
And I put "works" in quotation marks, because it's not really working. It probably makes things more difficult in the long run, or even the short run.
So, a few of the factors in why someone ends up addicted to one thing and not another:

ul: Do you have access to it?
What did you learn growing up as a way to deal with your stuff, and what did you learn was or wasn't acceptable?
What actually "works" for your particular stuck state, meaning what gives enough relief or reward that you seek it out again?
